x: The ground station One program holds the mission. It drives three vehicles over MAVLink, speaks the RoboCommand protocol to the judges, and keeps enough state that an interruption costs seconds rather than a run.

Architecture Vehicles talk MAVLink. The ground station talks MQTT and protocol buffers to RoboCommand. Between the two sits one orchestrator that owns every piece of mission state, and everything else reads from it: the terminal console, the three dimensional course view, and the protocol client. One orchestrator, several views. Only the RoboCommand client touches the course network, which is what handbook 3.4 requires: vehicles never connect to the judges' broker themselves. The adapter interface is the reason this works. A simulated vehicle, a firmware build running software in the loop and a real hull all implement the same adapter, so the mission code above them has never had to know which one it is driving.

Three state machines State lives in three places, each with one job. What each machine owns. Machine One per States Vehicle vehicle OFFLINE, BOOTING, READY, AUTONOMOUS, TASK_EXECUTING, RETURNING, EMERGENCY_STOP Task task attempt INACTIVE, QUEUED, ASSIGNED, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETE, FAILED, ABORTED Mission run IDLE, PRE_RUN_CHECK, RUNNING, EMERGENCY, COMPLETE Each task also carries an ordered list of steps, which is what the console shows as a previous, current and next triple. A step is the smallest thing the mission can be resumed at.

Interrupt and resume Task 4 is the reason the design looks like this. RoboCommand can interrupt a run at any moment with an assistance request, a keep-out zone or a moving vessel. The vehicle in the affected domain has to acknowledge on the wire, break off whatever it was doing, respond, and then carry on. When an incident arrives the orchestrator writes a checkpoint: the task, the step it reached, the progress through the step list and the score events already earned. The vehicle then runs the incident as its own task. When the incident clears, the checkpoint is restored and the vehicle picks up at the step it stopped on rather than at the start of the task. Your browser cannot play this video. Download it instead . A keep-out zone arrives mid transit. The console acknowledges it, the boat routes around the area, and the safe passage attempt resumes afterwards.

Health and escalation A heartbeat monitor watches every vehicle. Missed heartbeats and low battery raise alerts, and sustained heartbeat loss escalates to an emergency stop rather than waiting for an operator who may be looking at the water rather than the screen. Battery thresholds are per vehicle, because a quadrotor at 20 percent is a different problem from a boat at 20 percent. Before any run the console can run a pre-run gate: every vehicle reachable and in a ready state, every battery above its minimum, and all three domains present. It is non-destructive and can be run mid-mission.

The operator console The console is a terminal application, which is a deliberate choice: it runs over a shell connection from a laptop in a marquee on the promontory, it does not need a browser, and it redraws fine over a slow link. The layout is fixed so that an operator can find the same number in the same place under pressure. +- Header (clock) ------------------------------------------------------------+ | ROBOTX 2026 | IDLE -> [RUNNING] -> COMPLETE | Tier: ADVANCED | RC: * 04:12 | +--- USV ----------------+--- UUV ---------------+--- UAV ---------------------+ | USV > SAFE_PASSAGE | UUV | UAV > SAFE_PASSAGE | | READY -> [TASK_EXEC] | AUTONOMOUS | AUTONOMOUS -> [TASK_EXEC] | | Step: ROUTE_RELAY | Step: - | Step: [ROUTE_RELAY] | | Pos: 1.2834,103.8607 | Depth: 1.4 m | Alt: 42 m | | Batt: [#######...] 73% | Batt: [########..] 81%| Batt: [#########.] 92% | +- Task Prev -> [Current] -> Next Tier Vehicles ----------------+ | SAFE_PASSAGE ASSIGNED -> [IN_PROGRESS] ADV usv,uav | | Step: ROUTE_RELAY -> [TRANSIT_PASSAGE] -> EXIT_REPORT ########.. 72% | | INFRASTRUCTURE_SURVEY - -> [QUEUED] ADV uuv,uav | +- Incident panel (only while a Task 4 incident is live) ---------------------+ +- Health and alerts ------------------+- RoboCommand log --------------------+ | [OK ] USV heartbeat 8 ms | 14:22:01 -> DockingReport bay=2 | | [WARN] UAV battery low: 28.1% | 14:22:00 <- RxCommand run_start | +--------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+ F1 ESTOP F2 Abort F3 Pre-Check F4 Arm F5 T4-Core F6 T4-Adv F7 T4-Dis The same mission can be opened in a browser at the same time, which is the three dimensional view on the simulation page. The terminal stays the console; the browser is the picture of what it is doing.

The RoboCommand link Handbook 3.4 defines how teams report to the judges: MQTT over TCP on port 1883, protocol buffer payloads from RoboNation's schema release, four topics, and a run start handshake that gates the whole run. Our client implements it, and we have run it against RoboNation's own test server. The four topics, from handbook 3.4.7. Purpose Topic Direction Course configuration robocommand/robotx/course To us, retained Vehicle report robocommand/robotx/SUTD/<vehicle>/report From us Team request robocommand/robotx/SUTD/request From us Team command robocommand/robotx/SUTD/command To us Reports go out at 2 Hz per vehicle carrying state, position, speed, heading, roll, pitch, altitude or depth, current task and vehicle type, with flight phase added for the aircraft. Sequence numbers are per vehicle for reports and per team for requests, and a response quotes the sequence number of the message it answers. The run start sequence and the log it produced are on the proof of readiness page, step by step.

Design decisions Three machines rather than one A vehicle can be autonomous while its task is suspended and the mission is in an emergency. Collapsing those into one machine would need a state for every combination. Checkpoints outside the task machine A checkpoint has to survive the task machine being reset, because that is what an interruption does to it. Keeping it separate is what makes resume a data restore rather than a replay. Depth hold counts as autonomous Only for the underwater vehicle, which cannot hold a position it does not know. The rest of the fleet has to be in a real guided mode to count. Only the consumed streams are requested ArduPilot's default stream set would saturate a HaLow link. The adapter asks for position at 4 Hz and status at 1 Hz, and re-asks if telemetry stops. The ground station carries 154 automated tests covering the state machines, the orchestrator lifecycle, suspend and resume, the protocol end to end, the embedded broker, the course layout and the readiness rehearsal. Safe passage Ten buoys carry light beacons. Infrastructure survey and repair The ROV homes on the active pinger, follows the pipeline, calls each segment intact or damaged, and holds its magnetic probe on the damaged node. The repaired node then names the resource it needs, and the quadrotor flies it in. 3. Coordinated logistics The boat finds the green docking bay, docks, sprays the lit window until it turns green, then passes the delivery colour to the quadrotor. 4. Dynamic incident response RoboCommand interrupts the run with an assistance request, a keep-out zone or a moving vessel. The affected vehicle acknowledges on the wire, responds, then picks up the task it left at the step where it stopped.

t: The real firmware, on a laptop
x: The real firmware, on a laptop Software in the loop runs the exact firmware the vehicles run, compiled for the host: ArduRover with a motorboat model for the BlueBoat, ArduSub with a vectored model for the ROV, and Copter with a quad model for the aircraft. That gives us the behaviour that matters and none of the risk: real arming checks, real filter convergence, real guided navigation, real failsafes. Between the firmware and the ground station sits an emulator for the WiFi HaLow link, because the radio is part of the system. It adds fixed latency and jitter, random loss, a bandwidth cap and periodic outages. Link profiles. The fringe profile is the one that finds bugs. Profile Behaviour perfect No impairment. Used when a test is about something else. halow_near Short range, low latency, occasional loss. halow_typical The link we expect on the course. halow_fringe 60 ms of latency with 40 ms of jitter, 8 percent loss, 300 kbps, and a two second fade every 25 seconds. Under the fringe profile the health monitor escalates to an emergency stop on heartbeat loss, which is the correct behaviour and the reason the profile exists. It is also what led to the adapter requesting only the telemetry it consumes instead of ArduPilot's default stream set.

The course model Everything on the water is built from the handbook's build specifications, in metres: ten buoys with side and top light beacons, the pair of survey buoys with their colour indicators and pingers, a five section pipeline on stands with five magnetic light nodes, three docking bays with their windows and indicators, two 2 m delivery platforms with 65 cm circles in the specified colours, and the launch pad. Marina Bay Sands, the ArtScience lotus, the Flyer and the Helix Bridge are there because they are what the operator will actually be looking at. Your browser cannot play this video. The ROV at transit depth with the tether running up to the boat. The water is opaque on purpose: Marina Bay is a working harbour, and a camera above the surface would see nothing. The same scene has three other modes. It can mirror live RoboCommand traffic off a broker, read MAVLink telemetry straight off a vehicle or a software in the loop fleet, or be served by the running ground station so the terminal console and the browser show one mission. Contrast is a setting. A low sun over the bay puts a white band exactly where the buoys are, so every effect that costs contrast has a slider behind it, with one preset for reading the course and one for video.

End to end validation One command launches the fleet, runs a full scripted mission against it and prints a pass or fail table of 25 checks. It covers the sequence from a cold start to a stop: fleet ready with position, the pre-run gate, the course configuration and run declaration, arming against real prearm checks, run start, takeoff, task dispatch, buoy circling and the passage transit under guided navigation, an assistance request arriving mid transit, the checkpoint, the incident response with its acknowledgement on the wire, resume from the checkpoint, the safe passage report, task and mission completion, return to launch, and an emergency stop that disarms everything. The exit code gates continuous integration, so a change that breaks the mission breaks the build. The browser scene is checked the same way. A headless harness builds the whole world without a screen, flies the mission, and fails if a task does not complete, if the expected RoboCommand messages do not appear in order, if a chase camera loses its vehicle, or if the underwater chase camera comes above the surface.

The team MARVL is the Multi-Agent Robotics Vision and Learning Lab at the Singapore University of Technology and Design. RobotX 2026 is a lab-wide project across software, three vehicle builds and the safety case behind them.

Who we are MARVL works on mobile robotics, multi-robot coordination, planning and scheduling, computer vision and machine learning, with field robotics on marine, ground and aerial platforms. The lab has run surface and underwater vehicles in Singapore waters for several years, and RobotX 2026 is the first time all three domains are flown together as one system. The competition entry is a student team under the RoboNation eligibility rules: at least three quarters of the members are full-time students, and students do the engineering. Staff and alumni advise. Buoyancy test. The aircraft has to float and be recoverable after a ditching, so we put it in the pool and swam it back.

How the team is organised Work is split into four builds and three cross-cutting tracks. Everything meets at the ground station, which is the only piece of software that talks to all three vehicles and to RoboCommand. Vehicle builds One group per vehicle, each responsible for its own autopilot configuration, safety systems and proof of readiness package. Autonomy Mission orchestration, task state machines, the operator console and the simulation stack that all of it is tested against. Perception Buoy and pipeline detection, camera work on the ROV and the aircraft, and the datasets behind them. Safety and compliance Kill switch chains, failsafe behaviour, RF declarations, pilot licensing and the airworthiness case with CAAS.

Test record Three levels of testing, from a suite that runs in under a minute to flights and water work with the hardware. This page is the record of what has been run, what it was for and what came out of it.

How we test Hardware time is the scarce resource. A pool booking is a morning, a boat session is a day, and the aircraft needs a licensed pilot present. So anything that can be caught without hardware is caught without hardware, and field sessions are spent on the things only water and air can answer. Every commit The automated suite runs in about a minute and covers the mission logic, the protocol and the course model. Before a hardware session The same mission is flown against the real firmware over an emulated radio, end to end, with a pass or fail per stage. On the water and in the air Autonomy, safety systems and failsafes, recorded start to finish so the footage doubles as readiness evidence.

What testing changed Four results that changed the design rather than confirming it. The underwater vehicle has no position ArduSub refuses guided modes without a position estimate. Underwater that never arrives. Depth hold became an autonomous mode for that vehicle, and the survey is flown on heading and time with visual reacquisition. The default telemetry set floods the radio Running over the fringe link profile made it obvious. The adapter now asks for position at 4 Hz and status at 1 Hz and re-asks if telemetry stops, which is a few packets per second per vehicle. Arming is a waiting game The filter needs 20 to 40 seconds after boot before prearm passes, and the position prearm failure is the usual blocker on the boat. Arming retries for 90 seconds instead of failing the run. Guided waypoints still time out One check in the validation run fails: a guided waypoint on the boat does not report arrival inside its window, usually after the vehicle has been through an interruption. The mission still completes, so it is an acceptance window and a retry question rather than a navigation failure, and it is the next thing being worked on. The 2024 detector transfers in part The trained buoy model holds up on colour classes at 0.945 mAP@0.5, but the shape classes do not transfer, because the 2026 buoys carry light beacons rather than shapes.

Delivery mechanism flights: pick a tin, fly a route, release on a circle. One session with all three vehicles autonomous at the same time, reporting through the ground station to a local broker. 22 inch quadrotor Built in the lab around a Pixhawk 6C mini. It reads the buoy field from above, relays the route to the boat, and carries resource tins to the delivery platforms. It also has to float, because part of the course is water.

Airframe A custom 22 inch quadrotor. Carbon arms and plate, 22.4 by 8 inch two blade propellers, and foam flotation strapped along the arms and the body so the aircraft stays upright and recoverable after a ditching. Two configurations are declared: the base aircraft, and the base aircraft with the tin grabbing assembly fitted. Power and endurance Four 6S1P lithium ion packs in parallel, 4,500 mAh each, 18,000 mAh at 22.2 V in total. Flight testing at the delivery configuration mass gives about 18 minutes, so missions are planned to land by 15 with roughly three minutes in reserve. Control and telemetry The manual link is a RadioMaster transmitter with a built in ExpressLRS module, paired to a receiver on the aircraft. It is independent of the ground station: the pilot can take off, fly and land with the laptop switched off. The ground station runs Mission Planner for monitoring, mission upload and autonomous mission management, and the operator console reports the aircraft to RoboCommand at 2 Hz along with the other two vehicles. Manual link ExpressLRS 2.4 GHz, frequency hopping Transmit power 50 mW setting, about 0.08 W EIRP Telemetry 2.4 GHz to Mission Planner Flight modes Stabilise, AltHold, Loiter, Auto, Land, RTL Declared ceiling 50 m above mean sea level Geofence Polygon with a 4 m internal buffer Aircraft telemetry is also relayed for Singapore's network remote identification requirements, so the heartbeat has to carry a complete field set every time. That is one of the reasons the RoboCommand client fills flight phase, altitude and heading on every report rather than only when they change. The dedicated transmitter, assigned to this aircraft and the nominated pilot.

Failsafe behaviour What the aircraft does without being asked. Trigger Detection Response Manual link loss 5 s without valid input Land: controlled descent at the current position, disarm on touchdown Telemetry loss 5 s without a heartbeat Land, with the pilot keeping manual control throughout Navigation loss 5 s without position Land Geofence reached Polygon fence with a 4 m buffer Brake and hold at the boundary, in manual and in autonomous flight Ceiling reached Fence altitude limit Hold at the declared ceiling even when commanded above it Mission abort Ground station command or the pilot's mode switch Loiter or return to launch. A scored attempt does not resume after a manual takeover The emergency stop on the transmitter cuts the motors immediately and works on the ground and in the air. Used in flight it produces an uncontrolled descent, so it is reserved for the case where continued flight is the greater hazard. Marked handling areas, so the aircraft is only ever picked up where it is safe to.

Delivery payload Tasks 2 and 3 both end with a tin on a coloured circle. The delivery assembly is a removable tin grabbing mechanism of about 0.20 kg on an underside mount, powered from the main battery. The mount is drilled and the aircraft flies with it fitted; the grabber itself is the part still being finished. The delivery tins are aluminium cans of 40 to 50 g coated in red, green or blue. The platforms are 2 m squares with 60 to 70 cm circles in the handbook's specified colours, which is what the simulator draws and what the perception work targets.

BlueBoat The surface vessel runs the safe passage, docks and fights the window fire, and is the only vehicle that has to keep a status light visible at a hundred metres while doing it.

The platform A Blue Robotics BlueBoat: a 1.2 m catamaran with two thrusters, an ArduRover autopilot on a Pixhawk, and a companion computer that carries the WiFi HaLow link back to shore. The ground station drives it over MAVLink, so the boat is reached the same way in simulation, in software in the loop and on the water. Hull BlueBoat catamaran, 1.2 m Autopilot ArduRover on Pixhawk Autonomy modes GUIDED, with AUTO for surveys Ground link WiFi HaLow, MAVLink at 14550 Telemetry to shore Position 4 Hz, status 1 Hz Tow and lift points. Four marked points on the cross members, with a harness that takes the boat out of the water without loading the hulls.

Safety systems Section 5.2 of the handbook is specific about what a surface vessel has to carry, and all of it is on the boat. Handbook 5.2 requirements and how the boat meets them. How it is driven The ground station holds the boat in GUIDED and sends position targets, which is what the safe passage and the dock approach are built from. Arming goes through ArduPilot's own prearm checks with a retry, because the GPS prearm failure is the usual blocker on this hull and the retry is what turns a failed launch into a thirty second delay. Leaving autonomy ends scoring for an attempt under rule 5.1, so manual takeover is treated as an abort in the console rather than as a mode change: the run is marked not scoring and the operator sees it in the header. Task 3 adds two things on top of navigation: a dock approach that has to place the hull inside a bay, and a water jet aimed at a 25 cm window. Both are driven from the same task state machine as everything else, with a step per action, so a suspension in the middle of a dock approach resumes at the step it stopped on.

Perception The buoy detector is a YOLOv5s model trained on the MHSeals set, at 0.945 mAP@0.5 and 0.693 mAP@0.5:0.95 over 27 classes. The colour classes transfer directly to the 2026 light beacons; the shape classes do not, because the 2026 buoys carry lights rather than shapes. Camera to lidar fusion from the lab's earlier work sits at about 8 cm of range error with a systematic 8 to 9 cm lateral and vertical bias, which is the figure the passage transit planning is built around.

BlueROV2 The underwater vehicle surveys the pipeline and repairs it. It is also the vehicle that forced the most interesting design decision of the season, because it has no idea where it is.

The platform A BlueROV2 in the heavy configuration: six thrusters, an ArduSub autopilot on a Pixhawk, and a Raspberry Pi running BlueOS that carries video and MAVLink up the tether. Autonomy talks to it on one UDP endpoint while a pilot keeps QGroundControl on another, so a human can take the vehicle at any moment without the autonomy stack being torn down. Frame BlueROV2, 0.46 m, six thrusters Autopilot ArduSub on Pixhawk Companion Raspberry Pi, BlueOS at 192.168.2.2 Autonomy endpoint udpin 14551 Pilot endpoint udpin 14550, QGroundControl Camera RTSP H264, 1280x720 at 15 fps

No position underwater ArduSub refuses GUIDED and POSHOLD with "requires position" whenever the filter has no position estimate. In software in the loop that clears about a minute after boot, once the filter starts using GPS. On the real vehicle underwater it never clears, because a BlueROV2 without a Doppler log or an acoustic positioning system has no absolute position source at all. Rather than add hardware the budget does not have, the ground station treats depth hold as an autonomous mode for this vehicle only. The adapter asks for GUIDED first, falls back to depth hold when arming, and drives the vehicle with body frame velocity commands. Depth is closed by the autopilot, which is the one axis it can hold well without position. What this costs and what it buys The cost is that the survey is flown on heading and time rather than on waypoints, so the pipeline has to be reacquired visually rather than assumed. What it buys is a vehicle that is autonomous in the water on day one, with no dependency on a sensor that may not arrive.

Control interface Two ways into the vehicle, both through the same adapter. The two command paths and when each is used. Command What it does Used for VELOCITY Body frame velocity with yaw rate, in depth hold The normal autonomy path: transit, survey, station keeping RC_OVERRIDE Writes the same channels a pilot's transmitter writes, 1500 neutral, 1100 to 1900 full scale Fine positioning on the pipeline, and handing the vehicle back to a pilot mid-run Channels left unnamed in an override keep the pilot's stick values instead of being zeroed, which is what makes a hands-on-the-controller takeover work rather than fight the autonomy.

Pipeline survey and repair Task 2 starts at the buoy with the green indicator, which is the one with the active pinger below it. The vehicle descends, finds the pipeline, and reports each of the five segments as intact or damaged from that end. The damaged segment shows a red light ring with a magnetic switch at its centre; holding the probe there turns the light green. At Advanced the repaired node then flashes a colour for thirty seconds to name the resource it needs. The vehicle sends that request to the aircraft and reports completion to RoboCommand. At Disruptive the node flashes two colours, the first naming the tin and the second naming the delivery circle, and the request carries both. Rehearsing the survey. The chase camera holds below the surface while the vehicle is under, because Marina Bay is a working harbour and a camera above the water sees nothing.

Safety systems Onboard kill switch, with the vehicle positively buoyant when killed so it surfaces rather than sinks. Status light readable at about 80 m while surfaced, showing kill, manual and autonomous. Marked tow and lift points with a harness. A dedicated mounting location for the RJE ULB-350 locator beacon the event issues before any underwater vehicle enters the water, mounted vertically with the end cap down. Tether to the boat kept positively buoyant, under 6 m, and strong enough to recover the vehicle by pulling on it. Nothing attached to the vehicle is allowed to float on the surface during a scoring run, and the vehicle must not breach, which is why depth hold is armed before the run rather than after the first transit.

Building our own would have spent the season on watertight enclosures instead of on cross-domain autonomy, which is what the 2026 rules reward. A custom aircraft where it matters Nothing off the shelf carries a delivery mechanism, floats after a ditching and stays under 7 kg. The 22 inch airframe is built in the lab so the payload mount, the flotation and the battery layout are ours to change. One interface behind all three Every vehicle speaks MAVLink to the same adapter. Swapping a simulated vehicle for a firmware build or a real hull is a line in a configuration file, which is how the same mission code has been exercised since before the hardware arrived.
